clues: Early pre-Christian Greco-Roman traditions held a cardiocentric perspective, viewing the heart as the center of the soul, intelligence, and speech. Some believed that this was a result of injury that disrupted the 'vital heat' radiating from the heart.
The Edwin Smith Papyrus documented some of the earliest observations of this following traumatic head injuries around 1500 BC. Currently, strokes are the most common cause

A French physician, Pierre Paul Broca examined a patient who could only utter the syllable 'tan' after a brain injury, though his general intelligence and comprehension remained intact. Wernicke was heavily inspired by this work and described patients with impaired understanding but fluent and disordered speech. Both of these describe patients with different forms of this condition

This was first isolated in 1893 from a fungus, Penicillium brevicompactum. When culturing a fungus growing on bad corn, Bartolomeo Gosio noted that the fungus produced this active antibacterial compound. Unfortunately, this discovery was published in an obscure Italian medical journal and went unnoticed until much later and is not used as an antibiotic today

In the late 1980s, a South African geneticist was studying children with rare, severe immunodeficiencies. He noticed that when children lacked a specific enzyme to make guanosine, their T and B cells completely failed to multiply. He realized that this drug intentially mimics this exact defect.

This was approved by the FDA in 1995 and is increasingly utilized off label as a steroid sparing treatment in autoimmune diseases although was originally approved for the prevention of organ transplant rejection

The earliest known case of this was discovered in an Egyptian princess who lived between 1580 and 1550 BC. CT scans and studies of ancient Egyptian mummies show that roughly 34-50% of examined mummies had evidence of this.

John Hunter, an English surgeon, was one of the first to vividly describe the symptoms of this disease in the 18th century. He realized that his own attacks were brought on by rage, writing that his life was 'in the hands of any rascal who chose to annoy or tease him'. He tragically proved his theory right when he died suddenly after a heated argument during a hospital boards meeting
This is the most common type of heart disease and the leading cause of death worldwide
In 1907, there were only 25 documented cases of this disease in medical history. Now it accounts to approximately 200,000 hospital admissions each year in the United States

The incidence of this rose sharply when the industrial roller-milling process was introduced in the late 1800s. This process stripped the fiber, bran, and germ from grains to make fine, shelf-stable white flour. Indigenous populations in rural Africa almost never have this disease when eating traditional, plant-based, ultra-high-fiber diets.

Fidel Castro battled a case of this in 2006 that was complicated by bowel rupture and peritonitis. Although he required three surgeries, most uncomplicated cases are managed with supportive care based on the AVOD and DIABOLO trials
This was first described by an Australian pathologist in 1963 where he described 21 cases of children suffering from acute brain swelling and fatty liver failure

During nationwide outbreaks of influenza B and influenza A in the United States through the 1970s, hundreds of children each year, often recovering from flu or chickenpox and having taken a specific medication, suddenly began vomiting, experiencing personality changes or seizures, and slipping into comas. Case-fatality rates of this soared as high as 40%
In 1986, the FDA officially required warning labels on all over-the-counter aspirin products which led to a dramatic drop in reported cases of this condition
